keep: Temperament and compounding beat flash — and a monopoly's methods stain its monuments. Hold both.
lede: The calmest man in any room compounded oil, silence and Sundays into the largest fortune in American history.
copy: He began as an assistant bookkeeper who revered a clean ledger, and never stopped being one. Standard Oil, founded 1870, won refining not with better oil but with better arithmetic: relentless cost-shaving, secret railroad rebates, and the quiet offer competitors couldn't refuse — sell to us at our price, or be undersold until you do. By the early 1880s the trust controlled roughly ninety per cent of American refining, and had invented most of the machinery of the modern corporation along the way.

Ida Tarbell's 1904 investigative history made him the face of monopoly; the Supreme Court's 1911 breakup carved Standard into thirty-four companies — and, in the market's great joke, made him far richer, as the pieces outgrew the whole. His personal ledger, Ledger A, recording every cent given and spent from his first pay, survives: the temperament was the strategy.

The second act built modern philanthropy on the same operating system: give systematically, to root causes, through professional institutions. The University of Chicago, the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, and the hookworm campaign that reshaped Southern public health were run like Standard Oil — surveyed, staffed, measured. Both readings of the man are true at once, which is why he remains the case study for the question the Field Manuals circle: whether the engine can be taken without the cruelty.

bio.t: Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr.
bio.why: Immense, balanced, and alive to the double nature — the pious bookkeeper and the anaconda. The standard life, unlikely to be displaced soon.

contested: Chernow is judged fair but some historians find him gentler on the coercion than the record; Tarbell's classic prosecution brief has its own axe — Standard had ruined her father. Read Chernow and Tarbell against each other. The philanthropy's motives — atonement, system, or PR — remain argued, probably because all three are true.
